newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Chronology of Ecuador's political crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Ecuador's political crisis.

text.p: The following is a chronology of events in Ecuador's political crisis that led to the ouster of democratically elected President Abdala Bucaram and the appointment on Tuesday of Fabian Alarcon as interim president:
Jan. 8 - President Abdala Bucaram's administration launches austerity package, including stiff increases in electricity, gas and public transportation.
Feb. 5 - First day of a 48-hour general strike to protest the government's austerity measures. Demonstrators calling for Bucaram's resignation clash with police near presidential palace.

Feb. 6 - Trade unions extend walkout indefinitely or until Bucaram is dismissed. Army troops clash with demonstrators outside the presidential palace. Congress votes 44-34 to oust Bucaram on grounds of "mental incompetence," then swears in its leader Fabian Alarcon. Bucaram rejects the vote as "judicial barbarity," suggesting bid to depose him was engineered by economic elite.

Feb. 7 - Vice President Rosalia Arteaga declares her own right to the presidency as Ecuador wakes up with three "presidents." Defence minister declares state of emergency, which bars public demonstrations and suspends other individual guarantees. One person killed, scores injured in disturbances outside presidential palace as up to 4,000 protesters move to take the palace by force. Bucaram leaves to spend four-day carnival weekend in the Pacific coast city of Guayaquil .

Feb. 8 - Defence Minister Gen. Victor Bayas announces his resignation. Bucaram says he would rather die than step down in disgrace. Leading regional army chief Gen. Jose Grijalva says the military is not taking orders from Bucaram "since he is no longer in charge and was destituted by Congress."

Feb. 9 - Legislators and military leaders agree on a plan allowing Arteaga to take over as interim president for a few days until Congress passes legislation to reappoint Alarcon as president until Aug. 10, 1998. Bucaram concedes defeat, saying he was deposed in a military-backed "congressional coup" but vows to make a political comeback. Arteaga, formally appointed interim president, says the country "fortunately found a constitutional solution" to the crisis.

Feb. 10 - Arteaga throws cold water on "transition deal" saying Alarcon will be unable to assume the presidency until the Constitution is reformed to allow Congress to appoint presidents. Arteaga's adviser, Gil Barragan, says she made no deal and "will remain in power until there is a reform of the Constitution." Bucaram says he will call for a nationwide march on Feb. 26 toward Quito "to reinstate the president elected by the people."

Feb. 11 - Bucaram starts in Panama a regional tour to tell he was deposed in a "congressional coup." Arteaga says she will step aside once Congress elects a president. She leaves presidential palace after calling for a referendum within three months to fill the "constitutional void." Congress elects Alarcon by a 57-2 majority, with five abstentions and one blank vote.
